beats.intro: Module sixteen. [[sub]]Judging the credit of a company: its business, its financial ratios, and where its debt ranks.
beats.qual: Start with the business. [[bm]]A company with stable, predictable cash flows, low business risk, and little competition can carry more debt. [[ex]]Take BRWA, a carmaker shifting to electric vehicles over a decade. [[cp]]Its short-term commercial paper hardly feels that strategy. Investors mostly watch liquidity. [[five]]Holders of five year notes face growing competition and execution risk. [[fifteen]]Holders of fifteen year notes face the most, because their later payments depend on the strategy succeeding. [[gov]]Governance matters too. Highly rated issuers have few covenants. High yield issuers face restrictions on dividends and extra debt.
beats.collateral: Collateral is a second source of repayment. [[tan]]Secured lenders prefer tangible assets, like property, equipment, and inventory, over intangibles, like patents and goodwill. [[value]]Collateral matters most for weaker borrowers, when the probability of default is high. [[ex]]In two thousand twenty, a cruise line suspended operations, and raised three point three billion dollars of secured notes, backed by twenty eight of its ships. Pledging assets gave it cheaper, more available financing.
beats.quant: Quantitative analysis asks how likely the company is to meet its debt. [[a]]Forecasts can be top-down, starting from the economy, or bottom-up, starting from revenue drivers. [[prof]]Profitability: strong, stable operating earnings. [[lev]]Leverage: how much debt compared with earnings or assets. [[cov]]Coverage: earnings or cash flow compared with interest and debt service. [[liq]]And liquidity: cash and credit lines available for near-term payments. A firm can be solvent, yet fail for lack of liquidity.
beats.ratios: Credit analysts turn these into ratios. [[m]]EBIT margin: operating profit as a share of revenue. Higher is better. [[c]]EBIT to interest: how many times operating profit covers interest. Higher is better. [[l]]Debt to EBITDA: leverage. Higher means more risk. [[r]]Retained cash flow to net debt: cash flow after dividends, compared with debt net of cash. Higher is better. [[ex]]Compare two companies. Company Y has a higher margin, more coverage, lower leverage, and stronger cash flow. Y is the lower credit risk.
beats.seniority: Seniority decides who is paid first in default. [[sec]]Secured debt has a claim on specific assets, so it has a lower loss given default. First lien ranks highest, then second lien. [[uns]]Senior unsecured debt comes next. It is the most common corporate bond. [[sub]]Then subordinated and junior subordinated debt, which often recover little. [[gap]]If collateral is worth less than the secured claim, the shortfall becomes an unsecured claim. [[pari]]Bonds of the same rank are equal, whatever their maturity. [[rec]]Recoveries follow rank. In two thousand nineteen, defaulted senior secured bonds recovered about forty six percent, and senior unsecured about thirty one percent.
beats.issue: Rating agencies give two kinds of ratings. [[iss]]The issuer rating reflects the company's overall creditworthiness, and applies to its senior unsecured debt. [[isu]]An issue rating looks at a specific bond. [[not]]Secured debt may be rated higher than the issuer rating, and subordinated debt lower. [[ex]]For example, an issuer rated double B might have a senior secured bond one notch higher, and a subordinated bond two notches lower.
beats.wrap: Let's recap. [[w1]]The business model and industry shape a company's capacity for debt. [[w2]]Profitability, leverage, coverage, and liquidity drive default risk. [[w3]]Seniority and collateral drive loss given default. [[w4]]Issue ratings are notched from the issuer rating.
